The Quadratic Equations chapter is a high-yield part of the CAT Quantitative Aptitude section, and a favourite in XAT, SNAP, NMAT and CMAT too. This guide explains what CAT Quadratic Equations tests, the formulas and shortcuts worth memorising, the mistakes that cost marks, and a free 10-question online test you can take right now.

Take the quiz below first, read the explanation for anything you miss, then use the chapter e-book at the end for full, exam-level practice.

What CAT asks on Quadratic Equations

Roots and their nature (discriminant), Vieta’s sum/product relations, forming equations from roots and maxima/minima of quadratics.

Key formulas & shortcuts

  • Roots: x = (−b ± √(b²−4ac))/(2a); D = b²−4ac.
  • D>0 real distinct, D=0 real equal, D<0 complex.
  • Sum of roots = −b/a, product = c/a.
  • Equation with roots α, β: x² − (α+β)x + αβ = 0.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Sign errors in −b/a for the sum of roots.
  • Forgetting D=0 is the equal-roots (tangency) case.
  • Dropping the ± in the quadratic formula.

questions.q: If a,b,c are odd integers and ax²+bx+c=0 has real roots, then
questions.explanation: b²-4ac: an odd square is ≡1 (mod 8) and 4ac≡4 (mod 8), so the discriminant ≡5 (mod 8), which is never a perfect square. Hence the (real) roots are irrational.

questions.q: If x²+ax+bc=0 and x²+bx+ca=0 ( a≠ b ) have a common root, then their other roots satisfy
questions.explanation: Subtracting gives (a-b)x+c(b-a)=0⇒ x=c (common root). Then the other roots are b and a (from the products bc and ca ). The equation with roots a,b is x²-(a+b)x+ab; since a+b=-c, it is x²+cx+ab=0.

faq.q: What does the discriminant tell you?
faq.a: D>0 gives two real distinct roots, D=0 two equal roots, D<0 a complex conjugate pair.

faq.q: How to form a quadratic from its roots?
faq.a: Use x² − (sum)x + (product) = 0 with sum = α+β and product = αβ.
